title: An End-of-Year Survey for Measuring the Five Key Beliefs
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart shares a Google Forms survey created by Ohio educator Kristin Foxworth-O'Brien for measuring students' end-of-year standing on his five key beliefs framework (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy), offering it as a tool for gathering evidence-based reflection data as the disrupted 2019-2020 school year closed. He walks through each section of the survey — credibility (whether students see the teacher as effective), value (whether the learning felt meaningful), belonging (whether the work aligned with students' sense of identity), and combined effort/efficacy — explaining the purpose behind each set of questions. He highlights a short-answer question asking students how they personally define success, framing it as a way to surface the common but limiting belief that success equals grades and test scores. The piece closes by inviting readers to copy and adapt the form, framing it as part of learning as much as possible from the pandemic's disrupted "Phase 1" of remote teaching in order to prepare for whatever the fall would bring.
points: Stuart shares a ready-to-copy Google Forms survey (credited to Ohio educator Kristin Foxworth-O'Brien) built directly around his five key beliefs framework, turning theory into a concrete measurement tool.
The survey's structure — separate sections for credibility, value, belonging, and combined effort/efficacy — mirrors his broader framework, making it a direct classroom application of that theory.
He flags a short-answer question on how students personally define success as a way to surface and interrupt the common but limiting belief that success equals grades and test scores.
He frames the survey as part of reflecting on the pandemic's disrupted "Phase 1" of remote teaching, aimed at generating better data to prepare for uncertain fall reopening scenarios.
quotes: There's tons of science about human motivation, and in my work I've argued that a nice way of conceptualizing this science is in this idea: beliefs drive behavior.
Thankfully, Ohio educator Kristin Foxworth-O'Brien recently wrote to me with an excellent Google Forms survey she's giving her students as we approach the end of this crazy year. It's pretty simple.
The form starts with several questions on teacher credibility, all well-aligned with the CCPR of credibility. The goal here is to get a sense of whether my students thought of me as a good teacher.

I added a short answer question to this section to see how my students define success. A huge obstacle to the efficacy belief in schools is that our system tends to barrage students with the idea that success is measured by grades and tests.
I think a lot of us are thinking about how we can learn as much as possible from Phase 1 so that we're better prepared for whatever the fall looks like.
